Many folks want AR pistols (or SBRs), because of the compactness and weight, as well as the ability to more easily operate them efficiently within smaller spaces (defense of your home, defense of your vehicle, etc.) if necessary.

With a shorter barrel comes a loss in projectile velocity, muscle energy, and long range accuracy when comparing the same ammo in an appropriately long barrel, etc. Because this is a given, it’s a good idea to opt for a heavier projectile and not even plan to shoot at longer ranges. Many have opted for .300 BLK (300 blackout), assuming it fills this gap well. However, this round has similar muzzle energy to a .556, and doesn’t perform especially well out of really any barrel. The muzzle energy of both, out of a 10.5” barrel, varying by specific round of course, sits around 1600-1800 joules. Ammo for .300 BLK, .556, 7.72x39, and .308 typically comes with a spitzer tip, which is specifically for long range ballistic performance. Spitzer comes at the expense of reduced wound channel performance (cleanly sails through flesh with less damage), and reduced ability to hold its vector when it encounters anything in its path. For example, you are shooting at some thing in a wooded area and your bullet hits a small twig on its way, with a spitzer tip you will likely miss your target as a result, especially if the bullet is fairly long and narrow. This is also the reason you hear stories about people shooting a deer in the neck neck and having the bullet leave the bottom of its foot, etc. All of this is relevant with .556, .300 BLK, and .308. It’s even relevant with powerful rounds like .300 WM and .338 LM.

Another problem with using these rounds is that, because they are designed for distance, they are necessarily not designed to impart their energy immediately upon impact. This is why they “sail cleanly” through soft targets, as I mentioned above. You can buy defense / hunting rounds for all of these, Which replaced the Spitzer brass tap with a hollow point that is filled in with a rubber/plastic placeholder. This helps, but it is really just a Band-Aid. If you watch these rounds fired into ballistic gel, the wound channels are less impressive than you might expect.

The moral of the story is that all of these rounds are designed for speed and reaching your target at a long range; not so much for devastating your target.

If you are giving up long range accuracy by purchasing an SBR or AR pistol, why not go for a round that is specifically designed to devastate a target and that does not care about long range (+250yd) accuracy and which is designed specifically to be fired through a shorter barrel?

.458 SOCOM was designed to be all of these things.

.458 SOCOM was designed specifically to immediately incapacitate a human target with a single shot. It’s name is derived from its origin story; a group of special operators were sitting around at a barbecue discussing the fact that .556 required many shots to incapacitate an enemy during raids in the Middle East, partly due to these enemies chewing on Khat leaves, which basically meth them up before conflict. They wanted a round that would fit into the AR platform, but which would offer superior close range performance out of carbines and SBRs. What they came up with was a slightly modified .45-70 round, which fit single-file into a typical double-stack .556 magazine.

.458 SOCOM rounds range from the high 200s grain to 600 grain. If you shoot subsonic 600 grain, you will have the same muzzle energy as a supersonic .556 round, but a 600 grain .458 SOCOM will go through 2 car doors and still mulch your insides. If you don’t put a suppressor on, the high velocity rounds are preferable. For example, a Black Butterfly (highly recommended for .458 ammo) “TSX high velocity” round will absolutely shred a target and provides around 3500 joules of muzzle energy (about twice a .556), and is enough killing power to hunt a buffalo.

I recommend watching Black Butterfly’s ballistic gel videos on (((YouTube))). I also recommend looking up “.458 SOCOM bear hunt” and “.458 SOCOM deer hunt” to watch many large, full grown animals literally flip upside down dead, in situ, with single shot.

If you’re interested in buying a .458 SOCOM AR, I recommend Wilson Combat for a carbine length, or CMMG for a pistol or SBR.

Or, if you’re OK with putting an AR together yourself (easy, but requires a little patience, but then you can put in the best of everything, Geissele parts, trigger, etc.), I highly recommend purchasing your barrel and bolt from Tromix (the owner, Tony, was involved in the original design and made the first .458 SOCOM AR).

You only need all the same standard parts as any other AR, with the exception of the bolt in barrel needing to be .458 SOCOM, and one other exception: you’ll want an upper with a slightly larger ejection port to ensure you don’t ever have trouble ejecting the larger shells. CMMG makes such uppers, as does Gibbz Arms, Tromix, Wilson Combat, and a number of others.

You wouldn’t settle for a .22 or a .380 for your defense pistol. Don’t settle for .556 or .300 BLK for your defense AR.
